In Korean, sentences often follow a subject-object-verb (SOV) structure. To form a sentence:

The subject is placed at the beginning.
The object (if there is one) comes after the subject.
The verb comes at the end of the sentence.
For example:

"It is hot" in Korean is "덥습니다" (deopsseumnida), where "덥" (deop) means "hot," and "습니다" (seumnida) is a polite ending for the verb.
"I am hungry" in Korean is "배고픕니다" (baegopeumnida), where "배고프" (baegopeu) means "hungry," and "니다" (nida) is the polite form.
The use of polite endings is important in Korean to show respect, especially in formal settings. The verb endings can change based on the formality of the conversation.

The object (if there is one) comes after the subject.
The verb comes at the end of the sentence.
For example:

"It is hot" in Korean is "덥습니다" (deopsseumnida), where "덥" (deop) means "hot," and "습니다" (seumnida) is a polite ending for the verb.
"I am hungry" in Korean is "배고픕니다" (baegopeumnida), where "배고프" (baegopeu) means "hungry," and "니다" (nida) is the polite form.
The use of polite endings is important in Korean to show respect, especially in formal settings. The verb endings can change based on the formality of the conversation.
